Executive Statutory and Policy Overview of the Canadian R&D Tax Architecture

Canada maintains one of the most comprehensive and structurally mature research and development (R&D) fiscal incentive regimes among industrialized economies, anchored at the federal level by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Governed primarily by Section 37, Section 127, Section 127.1, and Subsection 248(1) of the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) (ITA), alongside Part XXIX (Section 2900) of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945) (ITR), the program is co-administered by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which executes technical reviews, financial audits, and administrative compliance.

Rather than operating as a discretionary grant subject to ministerial budget caps, the federal SR&ED regime functions as a statutory entitlement within the self-assessment tax system, delivering fiscal support through a dual-mechanism architecture. First, taxpayers may pool eligible current and capital SR&ED expenditures under Subsection 37(1) of the ITA to deduct them in full against business income in the current taxation year or carry them forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Second, taxpayers earn SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under Subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the ITA, which provide either a direct cash refund under Section 127.1, a reduction of Part I federal income tax payable, or a combination of both, with unused non-refundable credits eligible for a 3-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward.

Between late 2024 and early 2026, the Canadian federal SR&ED framework underwent its most consequential legislative transformation in over a decade. Initiated in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, expanded in Federal Budget 2025, detailed in the Department of Finance's August 2025 legislative proposals, and formally enacted into law upon the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, these statutory reforms apply retroactively and prospectively to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. The legislative overhaul directly addresses long-standing structural criticisms regarding Canada's over-reliance on narrow indirect tax credits and the erosion of fiscal support for scaling technology enterprises, capital-intensive R&D performers, and publicly traded Canadian innovators.

The post-December 15, 2024 legislative regime introduces four foundational structural shifts that reshape corporate R&D tax planning across Canada. First, the legislation doubles the annual qualified expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% federal ITC rate from $3 million to $6 million, thereby increasing the maximum annual refundable federal cash credit for qualifying corporations from $1.05 million to $2.1 million. Second, the statutory amendments expand eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC under Subsection 127(10.1) beyond Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) to include Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), eliminating the punitive fiscal cliff that historically penalized domestic technology companies upon executing an initial public offering (IPO) or listing on a public exchange.

Third, the legislation modernizes the corporate size phase-out thresholds and introduces an elective revenue-based metric. For CCPCs, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range under Subsection 127(10.2) is raised from the legacy $10 million to $50 million corridor to a substantially wider $15 million to $75 million corridor. Concurrently, ECPCs are governed by a three-year average annual revenue phase-out between $15 million and $75 million under Subsection 127(10.6), and CCPCs may now formally elect under Subsections 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) to calculate their expenditure limit using the ECPC revenue-based formula rather than taxable capital. This election prevents pre-revenue or early-stage venture-backed CCPCs with substantial equity capital on their balance sheets from losing access to the 35% refundable credit. Fourth, reversing the 2014 repeal effected by the Jobs and Growth Act, 2012 (Bill C-45), the legislation restores both capital expenditures for depreciable property and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, to the Subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the Subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base, including Shared-Use Equipment (SUE).

body.text: Statutory Definition of SR&ED and the CRA Eligibility Framework
Legislative Definition Under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The legal gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set forth in Subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which superseded the historical placement of the definition in Subsection 2900(1) of the ITR. Under the preamble to Subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statute bifurcates eligible core investigation into three primary pillars—basic research, applied research, and experimental development—complemented by a fourth pillar covering directly attributable support work.

Under Paragraph 248(1)(a), basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research typically occurs in laboratory or theoretical settings—frequently involving third-party payments to universities, research institutes, or scientific consortia—where hypotheses regarding fundamental phenomena, such as elementary particle properties or biochemical mechanisms, are formulated and experimentally tested without immediate commercial utility. Under Paragraph 248(1)(b), applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Because applied research shares a practical, application-driven orientation with experimental development, the administrative and judicial criteria governing experimental development generally extend to applied research claims.

Under Paragraph 248(1)(c), experimental development is defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In Canadian corporate tax practice, the vast majority of industrial SR&ED claims are filed under Paragraph 248(1)(c), relying on the statutory recognition that incremental improvements to existing technologies qualify for tax incentives provided they require resolving underlying technological uncertainty. Complementing these three core categories, Paragraph 248(1)(d) encompasses eligible support work, which is strictly limited to work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight enumerated disciplines—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in Paragraphs 248(1)(a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada.

A foundational legal constraint governs Paragraph 248(1)(d): activities falling within the eight enumerated categories never constitute SR&ED on a standalone basis. To qualify as eligible support work, the claimant must establish a dual statutory nexus demonstrating that the activity was performed directly in support of eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada, and that the scope, duration, and cost of the support activity were strictly commensurate with the technical needs of that core investigation.
Statutory Exclusions Under Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k) and Boundary Delineation

To prevent routine commercial, industrial, and pre-production expenses from migrating into the SR&ED tax credit base, Paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the definition in Subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude seven categories of activity from constituting SR&ED. Specifically, Paragraph 248(1)(e) excludes market research or sales promotion; Paragraph 248(1)(f) excludes quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; Paragraph 248(1)(g) excludes research in the social sciences or the humanities; Paragraph 248(1)(h) excludes prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; Paragraph 248(1)(i) excludes the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; Paragraph 248(1)(j) excludes style changes; and Paragraph 248(1)(k) excludes routine data collection. Collectively referred to as the statutory exclusions, these activities cannot be claimed even if they occur within an innovative enterprise, though the CRA instructs auditors that excluded work should only be delineated after confirming whether eligible core SR&ED work has been performed.

In technical audits, significant friction arises where an activity superficially resembles both an eligible support category under Paragraph 248(1)(d)—such as "testing" or "data collection"—and a statutory exclusion under Paragraphs 248(1)(f) or (k) for "routine testing" or "routine data collection". Under the CRA's administrative guidelines, the determinative criterion distinguishing eligible support work from excluded work is the underlying purpose of the activity. The auditor must evaluate why the specific work was executed. If data collection or testing is conducted specifically for the purpose of testing a scientific or technological hypothesis within an active experimental development project, it qualifies as eligible support work under Paragraph 248(1)(d). Conversely, if the identical testing protocol or data collection is executed to verify compliance with established regulatory standards, validate commercial production batches, or gather baseline market telemetry, it is statutorily barred under Paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (k). Furthermore, where a taxpayer conducts eligible SR&ED concurrently with excluded activities—such as developing a novel metallurgical extraction process while simultaneously prospecting for minerals—the eligible experimental development remains claimable, whereas the mineral prospecting costs must be strictly segregated and excluded under Paragraph 248(1)(h).
Evolution of CRA Administrative Policy: From the Five Questions to the Why and How Guidelines

Historically, the CRA evaluated SR&ED project eligibility through Information Circular 86-4R3 (dated May 24, 1994) and subsequently through the 2012 and 2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy, which operationalized the five sequential questions articulated by the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen. Prior to 2014, the CRA also frequently summarized these requirements into three classic criteria: technological uncertainties, systematic work, and technological advancements. On August 13, 2021, the CRA replaced the 2015 policy document with the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives.

While the underlying statutory law and judicial precedent remain unchanged, the 2021 Guidelines reorganize the eligibility analysis around two overarching statutory requirements derived directly from the preamble and paragraphs of Subsection 248(1): Why the work was conducted, and How the work was conducted. Both requirements must be concurrently satisfied for a project to qualify for SR&ED tax incentives.

The recognition that a scientific or technological uncertainty exists marks the starting point (impetus) of SR&ED, while the advancement of knowledge or capability is the targeted outcome. Resolving uncertainty requires generating or discovering new knowledge beyond available public or proprietary know-how.

Encompasses Question 2 (Formulating hypotheses), Question 3 (Systematic investigation via experiment or analysis), and Question 5 (Contemporaneous record-keeping as work progresses).

Requires a disciplined four-stage process: (1) generating an idea/hypothesis consistent with known facts; (2) testing the hypothesis via experiment or analysis; (3) developing logical conclusions from results; and (4) keeping evidence generated as the work progresses.

body.text: Under the "Why" requirement, the recognition that scientific or technological uncertainty exists marks the starting point for SR&ED work, whereas the advancement is the targeted outcome; thus, an attempt to resolve technological uncertainty is inherently an attempt to achieve technological advancement. The CRA explicitly notes that indicators of insufficient existing technological knowledge include situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, performance requirements or specifications do not conform to existing engineering standards, excessive interacting variables or unknowns prevent predictable modelling, operating parameters or conditions fall outside the normal operating range, or the technical nature of the problem evolves dynamically during investigation. Crucially, the CRA Guidelines emphasize that merely acquiring existing knowledge or know-how—whether through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring external domain experts or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—does not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve technological advancement and therefore fails the "Why" requirement.

Under the "How" requirement, the claimant must demonstrate that the investigation followed a systematic methodology executed by means of experiment or analysis. This systematic methodology comprises generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving the problem; testing that idea or hypothesis through structured experiment or analysis, recognizing that the hypothesis may evolve and change as a result of testing; developing logical conclusions based on the empirical results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.
Federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Mechanics: Deductions, Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability
Subsection 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Subsection 37(1) of the ITA establishes a specialized tax account known as the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Unlike ordinary business expenses deducted annually in computing income from a business or property under Subsection 9(1) or prohibited from immediate deduction as capital outlays under Section 18, eligible SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada are aggregated into the Subsection 37(1) pool.

The pool balance is calculated dynamically each taxation year through statutory additions and reductions. On the additions side, Paragraph 37(1)(a) adds current SR&ED expenditures incurred in the year, encompassing direct salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed, eligible equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, and—for taxpayers electing the traditional overhead method—actual overhead expenditures directly related and incremental to SR&ED. Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) adds current expenditures incurred on the taxpayer's behalf through subcontracts, while Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1) includes eligible third-party payments to corporations or approved research entities. For depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, capital expenditures meeting the all-or-substantially-all (ASA) test are restored to the pool under Paragraph 37(1)(b). Additionally, Paragraph 37(1)(c) adds any repayments made by the taxpayer in the year of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool.

On the reductions side, Paragraph 37(1)(d) mandates that the pool be reduced by all government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED at the filing deadline. Paragraph 37(1)(d.1) further reduces the pool by any provincial super-allowance benefit amount. Furthermore, federal SR&ED ITCs claimed or refunded in a taxation year reduce the Subsection 37(1) pool in the subsequent taxation year. Any remaining positive balance in the Subsection 37(1) pool may be deducted in whole or in part to reduce income for tax purposes in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to be deducted against income for tax purposes in any future taxation year. This indefinite carryforward mechanism is particularly valuable for early-stage technology enterprises that seek to preserve non-capital loss balances or defer tax deductions until they reach commercial profitability.
Section 127 Investment Tax Credit Rates and Entity Classifications

The financial core of the federal SR&ED program is the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) governed by Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA. The ITC is calculated as a statutory percentage of the claimant's "qualified expenditure" for the taxation year as defined in Subsection 127(9). Both the credit rate and the cash refundability percentage depend strictly on the legal classification of the claimant and whether the expenditures fall within the corporation's annual expenditure limit.

body.text: Under Subsection 127(9), the basic SR&ED ITC rate is 15%, which applies to corporations that do not qualify as CCPCs or ECPCs, to CCPCs and ECPCs on qualified expenditures exceeding their annual expenditure limit, and to individuals (sole proprietorships), partners of partnerships, and beneficiaries of trusts. Under Subsection 127(10.1), CCPCs and—for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024—ECPCs earn an enhanced 20% ITC in addition to the 15% basic rate, yielding a combined 35% ITC rate on qualified expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit.

Under Subsection 127.1(2.01), for a CCPC (as well as an ECPC under the amended provisions) on qualified current expenditures within its expenditure limit, the refundability rate of the 35% ITC is 100%, while restored capital expenditures within the expenditure limit are refunded at 40%. For qualified expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit, a CCPC that meets the definition of a "qualifying corporation" under Subsection 127.1(2) earns a 40% cash refund on its 15% basic ITC, whereas non-qualifying CCPCs and other corporations earn a non-refundable 15% ITC. Furthermore, no amount is included in a claimant's ITC in respect of an SR&ED expenditure made in the course of earning income that is exempt from Part I tax. Under Subsection 127(5) and Subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC that is refunded in cash in the taxation year is deemed to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in the year, thereby reducing the remaining ITC pool available for the 3-year carryback or 20-year carryforward.
Expenditure Limits, Phase-Out Formulas, and Corporate Group Allocations

Under Subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA, the enhanced 20% top-up credit (yielding the combined 35% rate) applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual "expenditure limit". Following the enactment of Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026), the maximum expenditure limit for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, is $6,000,000, doubled from the pre-December 16, 2024 limit of $3,000,000. Practitioners reviewing historical legislative files should note that while the August 2025 Department of Finance explanatory notes initially referenced an interim $4.5 million figure in commentary on Subsection 127(10.6), Federal Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 established the enacted statutory limit at $6 million across both Subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6).
CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Subsection 127(10.2) ITA)

Unless a CCPC makes a revenue-method election, its $6 million expenditure limit is determined under Subsection 127(10.2) based on the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and any associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year. For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the phase-out begins at $15 million of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada and reaches nil at $75 million, replacing the narrower $10 million to $50 million corridor that applied to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024. The statutory formula under amended Subsection 127(10.2) is:
$6 million × [($60 million − A) ÷ $60 million]

where A is the amount by which the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and its associated corporations) exceeds $15 million, with A = 0 if taxable capital is $15 million or less, and capped at $60 million when taxable capital reaches $75 million. Consequently, the $6 million expenditure limit drops on a straight-line basis by $100,000 for every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $15 million.

Tax auditors and corporate controllers must carefully distinguish the modernized SR&ED taxable capital phase-out from the federal Small Business Deduction (SBD) business limit phase-out. The federal SBD business limit of $500,000 continues to shrink over the narrower $10 million to $50 million prior-year taxable capital range (and is additionally subject to the $50,000 passive investment income grind and proration for short taxation years under 51 weeks), whereas the SR&ED expenditure limit utilizes the expanded $15 million to $75 million corridor.
ECPC Revenue-Based Phase-Out and the CCPC Election (Subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.31), and 127(10.32) ITA)

For an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC), Subsection 127(10.6) determines the $6 million expenditure limit using the corporation's average annual gross revenue reflected in its financial statements over the three preceding fiscal years, aggregated across all corporations that are members of a consolidated group for the taxation year regardless of whether those corporations were associated or consolidated throughout the entirety of that three-year lookback period. The ECPC expenditure limit begins to shrink when three-year average annual revenue reaches $15 million and is completely eliminated when three-year average annual revenue reaches $75 million.

Crucially, under new Subsections 127(10.31) (for a standalone CCPC) and 127(10.32) (for a group of associated CCPCs), a CCPC may formally elect to opt out of the taxable capital test in Subsection 127(10.2) and instead compute its expenditure limit under the ECPC three-year average annual revenue test in Subsection 127(10.6). Where this election is filed for a taxation year, the expenditure limit based on taxable capital employed in Canada under Subsection 127(10.2) does not apply to the corporation or associated group for that year. Because taxable capital employed in Canada includes raised equity capital less accumulated deficits plus associated companies' capital, venture-backed CCPCs in capital-intensive sectors frequently exceed $15 million—or even $75 million—in taxable capital immediately after a large financing round while generating minimal commercial revenue. By filing the Subsection 127(10.31) or (10.32) election, such a CCPC preserves its full $6 million expenditure limit and $2.1 million annual refundable cash credit so long as its three-year average annual revenue remains at or below $15 million.
Associated CCPCs and Consolidated ECPCs

Where CCPCs are associated within the meaning of the ITA, Subsection 127(10.21) mandates that the associated group share a single $6 million expenditure limit, and Subsection 127(10.3) requires the group to file an allocation agreement (Schedule 49) with the Minister of National Revenue before any member claims the enhanced credit. Ignoring the association rules causes the corporate group to exceed a limit it was statutorily required to share, triggering assessment adjustments. Parallel statutory mechanics govern consolidated groups of ECPCs under Subsection 127(10.61), which parallels Subsection 127(10.21) in requiring the group to share the maximum expenditure limit, Subsection 127(10.62), which parallels Subsection 127(10.3) in allowing the consolidated group to file an election allocating the limit among ECPC members, and Subsection 127(10.63), which addresses failure to file an allocation agreement.

General expenditure limit determination rules for short taxation years, multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year where a CCPC is associated in two or more of those tax years with another CCPC, and specific relieving provisions (where at least one shareholder of one corporation is not a shareholder of the other and such shareholding was not established to satisfy the relieving provision) are governed by Subsections 127(10.5) (renumbered from former Subsection 127(10.6)) and 127(10.64). Furthermore, Paragraph 87(2)(j.6) enforces continuity rules upon corporate amalgamation, deeming the new corporation formed as a result of an amalgamation to be the same corporation as, and a continuation of, each predecessor corporation for the purposes of Subsection 127(10.2).
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures, Overhead Methodologies, and Cost Inclusion Rules

To enter the Subsection 127(9) definition of "qualified expenditure", costs must fall within specific statutory categories and satisfy strict timing, residency, and nexus conditions. Further additions to the investment tax credit in respect of repayments of assistance are governed by Subsection 127(10.7) and Paragraphs (e.1) and (e.2) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in Subsection 127(9).
Direct Salaries, Wages, and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages paid to employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada constitute the primary expenditure base for most claimants. To qualify, the remuneration must represent salary or wages incurred in the taxation year and must be actually paid by the end of the taxation year or no later than 180 days after the end of the taxation year pursuant to Subsection 78(4) of the ITA. If unpaid remuneration is not discharged within 180 days of year-end, it cannot be included in the current year's SR&ED claim and may only be claimed in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid. Taxable benefits under Section 6 and employee stock option benefits under Section 7 of the ITA are statutorily excluded from eligible SR&ED salaries and wages.

Where a claimant incurs salaries or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada by Canadian-resident employees—which must be specifically disclosed on Line 265 of Form T661—the ITA restricts the permissible foreign salary claim to a maximum of 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages incurred for SR&ED work performed in Canada during the taxation year.
Restrictions on Specified Employees (ITR Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(9))

Stringent anti-avoidance caps apply to "specified employees"—defined in the ITA as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation. Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy and Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(9) of the ITR, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, Section 6 taxable benefits, Section 7 stock option benefits, and prior-year unpaid salary or wages paid in the year are completely excluded from both direct SR&ED wage claims and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary base for specified employees, and direct SR&ED salary is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE).

When calculating the salary base for the 55% PPA overhead method, Subsection 2900(7) of the ITR restricts the maximum amount that a claimant can include in the salary base for each specified employee to the lesser of two statutory thresholds. The first threshold is 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year, combining both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties while excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior year's unpaid salary or wages paid in the year. The second threshold is 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined for purposes of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days of employment in the taxation year under the following statutory formula:

where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual. Notably, there is no proration for the time during the year that the employee was not a specified employee. Furthermore, where a specified employee of a corporation is also employed by an associated corporation during the year, special allocation rules apply across the associated group, requiring the filing of Form T1174 to allocate the maximum specified employee salary cap among the associated employers.
Overhead Calculation: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Versus Traditional Method

Taxpayers must elect on Form T661 to claim SR&ED overhead and other expenditures using either the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method (the proxy method) or the Traditional Method. The choice of method applies across all SR&ED projects of the taxpayer for the entire taxation year.
Verification of the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount Rate

A frequent and costly technical error in outdated secondary literature is the assertion that the PPA rate is 65% or 60% of the salary base. Under Subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations—as amended following the Jobs and Growth Act, 2012 (Bill C-45, S.C. 2012, c. 31)—the PPA percentage was 65% for 2012 and prior years, 60% for the 2013 transitional year, and has been statutorily fixed at 55% of the SR&ED salary base since 2014. Using a 65% proxy rate on a 2026 filing overstates the proxy overhead by 10 percentage points and results in an immediate downward correction upon CRA assessment.

The PPA is computed in Part 5 of Form T661 pursuant to Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) to (VI) and Paragraph (b) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in Subsection 127(9) of the ITA, alongside Subsection 2900(4) of the ITR. Because the PPA is a notional amount that replaces actual overhead, it counts exclusively toward the Section 127 ITC calculation and does not enter the Subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Instead, the actual overhead and other expenditures that the PPA represents are deducted by the taxpayer as ordinary business expenses in computing net income under Subsection 9(1) of the ITA. Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the claimant does not calculate the salary base, the PPA in Part 5, or the overall cap; instead, the claimant must specifically identify, track, allocate, and substantiate which actual overhead and other expenditures—such as travel, training, property taxes, maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment, and incremental cloud computing—were directly related to performing SR&ED and would not have been incurred had SR&ED not been carried out.

body.text: Materials Consumed or Transformed, Subcontractor Payments, and Third-Party Payments
Materials Consumed or Transformed

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, expenditures for materials qualify for both the Subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the Subsection 127(9) ITC calculation if the materials are either consumed in, or transformed by, the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed refer to substances or components destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during experimental trials, whereas materials transformed refer to physical inputs integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom test rig during the SR&ED process. However, if an experimental prototype or transformed material is subsequently sold commercially or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED recapture rules in the ITA claw back the associated ITCs so that commercial inventory is not subsidized by R&D credits.
Subcontractor (Contract) Expenditures

Payments made to contractors for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant in Canada (reported on Lines 267 to 269 of Form T661, distinct from collaborative joint efforts or work performed by the claimant on behalf of another party reported on Line 266) are governed by distinct statutory rules depending on whether the parties deal at arm's length. Arm's-length contracts must be paid or payable to a "taxable supplier" in respect of SR&ED performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf. While 100% of the eligible arm's-length contract expenditure enters the Subsection 37(1) deductible pool under Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), Subsection 127(9) restricts the inclusion in "qualified expenditure" for ITC purposes to 80% of the contract cost. Conversely, non-arm's-length contract payments may be deductible in the pool if the underlying work qualifies, but they do not earn an ITC in the hands of the payer unless the non-arm's-length performer and payer file a joint agreement on Form T1146 to transfer the performer's qualified expenditures to the payer, in which case the performer must report the agreed transferred amount on Line 540 of Form T661.
Third-Party Payments

Under Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1) of the ITA, a taxpayer may claim third-party payments made to a corporation resident in Canada or to an approved university, college, research institute, or other non-profit R&D organization or consortium for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to a business of the taxpayer, provided the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results. Claimants must report each third-party payment on Form T1263, and—consistent with arm's-length contract rules—expenditures of a capital nature for depreciable property acquired by the third party before December 16, 2024, are excluded, whereas amounts related to depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, are eligible to be included on Line 535.
Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Lease Costs, and Shared-Use Equipment

From January 1, 2014, through December 15, 2024, capital expenditures and equipment lease costs were statutorily excluded from the SR&ED program following the repeal of Paragraph 37(1)(b) by the Jobs and Growth Act, 2012. Pursuant to the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, Budget 2025, and Bill C-15, capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, are once again eligible for both the Subsection 37(1) deduction pool and Section 127 SR&ED ITCs.

Under the CRA's updated administrative guidelines, an eligible SR&ED capital expenditure (entered on Line 390 of Form T661, which also captures expenditures for used equipment) is an expenditure made to acquire new or used depreciable property available for use after December 15, 2024, that the claimant intended to use in one of two ways: either to use all or substantially all (ASA — defined as 90% or more) of the operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value to perform SR&ED in Canada. Non-depreciable assets (such as land), buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, inventory, and goodwill are strictly excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures. Furthermore, any capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 enter the Subsection 37(1) pool and must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 for regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA), and subsequent disposition or conversion to commercial use may trigger recapture of CCA reported on Line 440.

Where depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, does not meet the 90% ASA test because it is utilized for both commercial operations and SR&ED, the claimant may still include a portion of the capital cost in its SR&ED ITC calculation if the asset qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), reported on Line 504 of Form T661. The SR&ED ITC calculation for SUE is identical under both the traditional method and the proxy method. The capital cost of SUE does not enter the Subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the taxpayer must depreciate the capital cost under the regular CCA rates and rules on Schedule T2SCH8. If the equipment is used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) in SR&ED in Canada during the statutory periods, the claimant may claim on Line 504 25% of the capital cost of the equipment in the first period (first-term SUE) and the other 25% of the capital cost in the second period (second-term SUE).

Additionally, lease costs of equipment incurred after December 15, 2024, qualify for SR&ED tax incentives where the underlying depreciable property was acquired after December 15, 2024. Generally, operating time means the time the equipment usually runs or functions; if a claimant's taxation year began before December 16, 2024, and straddles that date, SR&ED use is calculated as a percentage of the total operating time after December 15, 2024, while any lease costs incurred before December 16, 2024, remain strictly ineligible.
Judicial Precedents and Tax Court of Canada Jurisprudence

Because the statutory definition of SR&ED in Subsection 248(1) relies on qualitative scientific concepts rather than mechanical financial formulas, Canadian jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) serves as the binding interpretive framework for audits and litigation.
Foundational Appellate Authority: Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, and C.W. Agencies

The cornerstone of Canadian SR&ED case law is Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), authored by Justice Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada). In assessing physical hydraulic scale modelling conducted to solve fluid dynamics and river engineering challenges, Justice Bowman reviewed Information Circular 86-4R3 (dated May 24, 1994), observed that it was a generally useful and reliable guide, and emphasized that the SR&ED provisions of the ITA are incentive legislation requiring such fair, large, and liberal interpretation as best ensures the attainment of Parliament's objects. At paragraph 16 of Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman established the five canonical criteria (questions) for determining whether a particular activity constitutes SR&ED:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?
Did the process result in a technological advancement?
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: In Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman articulated three durable legal doctrines that govern technical reviews to this day. First, implicit in the term "technical risk or uncertainty" is the requirement that it be a type of uncertainty that cannot be removed by "routine engineering or standard procedures"—which describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. Second, even where individual components or mechanisms are known, system uncertainty can arise when integrating those components into a complex unified system produces unpredictable interactions. Third, the fourth question—whether the process resulted in a technological advancement—may be answered in the affirmative if the process at issue resulted in an advancement of general understanding recognizable to experts in the field, including the conclusive rejection of a hypothesis that demonstrates a particular technical avenue will not work.

Justice Bowman's five criteria were subsequently approved and elevated to binding appellate law by the Federal Court of Appeal in two landmark decisions. In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), the Federal Court of Appeal formally endorsed the Northwest Hydraulic framework and underscored the importance of contemporaneous documentation of experimental tests and results to prove scientific repeatability. Subsequently, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (Docket A-601-00, delivered December 11, 2001, by Justice Sexton, affirming Judge Bonner's Tax Court decision in 2000 DTC 2372), the Federal Court of Appeal summarized the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria at paragraph 17 and dismissed the taxpayer's appeal for the 1991–1995 taxation years.

In C.W. Agencies, the appellant marketed lottery tickets internationally by telephone and computer in multiple languages to two to three million customers, recording up to 25,000 purchases per day in its computer system. Balancing the appellant's testimony against the Crown's expert witness, the Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal concluded that the software development did not constitute SR&ED under Regulation 2900, characterizing the investigations as "those of competent and prudent users of complex, commercially available technologies rather than those of researchers seeking to discover new knowledge, concepts or principles". C.W. Agencies remains the primary authority relied upon by CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) when disallowing claims involving complex enterprise software integration, database scaling, and custom application engineering.
The Objective Standard of Technological Uncertainty in Modern Case Law

A pronounced trend in recent Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence (2019–2025) is the strict judicial enforcement of the rule that technological uncertainty is an objective test, not a subjective test. Claimants consistently lose appeals when they equate their own internal lack of familiarity, training, or engineering credentials with objective technological uncertainty.

Summarized the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as appellate law; ruled that complex software development by competent users of commercially available tools is routine engineering, not SR&ED.

Clarified that Criterion 5 (contemporaneous written records) is not an explicit statutory condition in the ITA or ITR, though records remain the primary evidentiary proof of systematic investigation.

Taxpayer lost; held that a company working outside its core trade must prove objectively that the technical risks could not be overcome by standard procedures accessible to competent professionals in the target field.

Taxpayer won; held that unpredictable interactions among identical ingredients in varying combinations/quantities constituted valid technological uncertainty, and credible CEO oral testimony bridged documentary gaps.

Taxpayer lost; held that "the mere fact that a product does not exist does not necessarily support the inference that its development involves technological or scientific uncertainty", and noted the fatal absence of expert evidence defining the state of the art.

Taxpayer won; applied the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria, finding on a balance of probabilities that the claimant faced objective technical uncertainty, adopted the scientific method, and achieved an advancement in general understanding.

body.text: In Dave's Diesel Inc. (2022), the appellant rested its case on the subjective knowledge of four non-engineers and non-mechanics who worked on the project; because they lacked formal engineering training, every aspect of the project appeared to them to be a technological uncertainty. The Tax Court firmly rejected this subjective approach, observing at paragraph 28 that if technological uncertainty were measured by the claimant's subjective knowledge, a grade school student attempting to build a simple electric motor would satisfy the statutory test. Similarly, in JEC Distributors Inc. (2022), where the appellant's expertise lay in welding technology rather than the target domain, the Court held at paragraph 22 that the test is strictly objective: the taxpayer must demonstrate that the risks could not be overcome by routine engineering or standard procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in the relevant field. In Logic Data Products Inc. (2021), the Court likewise held at paragraph 68 that knowledge and experience in the broader solar power industry regarding solar shingles governed whether an uncertainty was genuinely technological.

Furthermore, in Paveit Construction Inc. (September 2025), the Tax Court underscored at paragraphs 38 and 40 that the mere fact that a commercial product does not yet exist on the market does not support an inference that its development entails scientific or technological uncertainty, adding that the failure to lead expert evidence left the Court unable to distinguish alleged system uncertainty from routine engineering. Conversely, in Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 35) and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025 TCC), the taxpayers succeeded because they objectively demonstrated how the unpredictability of ingredient interactions in varying combinations and thermal processing parameters defied standard food science methodologies, adopted the scientific method to test hypotheses, and achieved advancements in general understanding.
Evidentiary Burden and Contemporaneous Documentation Standards

A nuanced legal distinction exists regarding the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion—whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed. In Northwest Hydraulic (at paragraph 16), Justice Bowman stated that a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results must be kept as the work progresses. However, as the Tax Court subsequently clarified in Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 42, at paragraph 118), Les Abeilles (at paragraph 65), and Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 35), keeping contemporaneous written documentation is not explicitly mandated as a standalone statutory condition in the ITA or the ITR. In Canafric, the Tax Court reiterated that documentary evidence is not always indispensable where credible, detailed oral testimony from company leadership (its CEO, Mr. Pandya) bridges gaps in the written experimental record.

Nevertheless, from an administrative audit and risk-management perspective, relying on retroactive reconstruction or oral testimony during a CRA review is hazardous. The CRA's 2021 Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives explicitly embed "keeping evidence that is generated as the work progresses" into the fourth step of the "How" requirement, and point out that if a study's end results cannot be measured or counted, the work may not be considered SR&ED. During an audit, CRA Research and Technology Advisors expect dated, contemporaneous experimental records—alongside project time sheets, financial statements, receipts, invoices, payroll records, and subcontractor contracts—to substantiate that hypotheses were formulated and tested systematically rather than constructed after the fact.
Administrative Filing Procedures, Statutory Deadlines, and CRA Audit Governance
Mandatory Tax Forms and Technical Narrative Architecture on Form T661

To access both the Subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the Section 127 ITC, a claimant must complete and submit prescribed forms containing prescribed information to the CRA by the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline. Every corporate claimant must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) as part of its T2 Corporation Income Tax Return, whereas individuals (sole proprietorships) must file Form T661 alongside Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)). Depending on the claimant's corporate structure and transactions, additional prescribed forms must be filed: Form T1145 (to allocate assistance between non-arm's-length parties), Form T1146 (to transfer qualified expenditures on non-arm's-length SR&ED contracts), Form T1174 (to allocate specified employee salaries among associated corporations), Form T1263 (to report third-party payments for SR&ED), and Schedule T2SCH49 (to allocate the expenditure limit among associated CCPCs under Subsection 127(10.3)). Corporations using CRA-approved commercial tax preparation software may submit their SR&ED claims electronically via Corporation Internet Filing, which is mandatory for most corporations under the ITA.
Technical Narrative Constraints on Part 2, Section B of Form T661

In Part 2, Section B of Form T661, the claimant must provide project-by-project technical descriptions that establish how the claimed work satisfies the statutory definition of SR&ED in Subsection 248(1). The CRA defines an "SR&ED project" as a set of interrelated activities that collectively are necessary to resolve scientific or technological uncertainties in an attempt to achieve specific scientific or technological advancements, pursued through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals. Failure to provide the prescribed project information results in the disallowance of the claimed expenditures. Part 2, Section B is structured around three mandatory technical questions, each governed by a strict 350-word maximum limit:

cells: What scientific or technological uncertainties did you attempt to overcome?
Describe the scientific or technological uncertainty encountered that led to the SR&ED, establishing why standard engineering or accessible knowledge was insufficient.
What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the technological obstacles/uncertainties described in Line 242?

Clearly demonstrate the systematic nature of the investigation in the tax year by describing the hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainties, the experiments and/or analysis conducted to test the hypotheses, the results obtained, and the conclusions drawn.
What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve or attempt to achieve as a result of the work described in Line 244?
Articulate the new scientific or technological knowledge generated or attempted as a result of the systematic investigation described in Line 244.

body.text: CRA Guide T4088 emphasizes that because Section B responses are strictly word-limited, narratives must be written in clear, concise technical language by personnel who performed, supervised, or are intimately familiar with the engineering or scientific work, avoiding vague marketing descriptions that trigger audit selection. In addition to the technical narratives, Lines 253 to 259 of Form T661 require mandatory disclosure of who prepared the Section B responses: Line 253 and Line 254 identify a directly involved employee who performed or directly supervised the SR&ED work described at Line 244; Line 255 and Line 256 identify another internal employee of the company not directly involved in the project; and Lines 257, 258, and 259 identify an external consultant along with the consultant's name and firm. Lines 260 and 261 require listing the names, relevant technical qualifications or experience, and position titles of up to three key individuals directly involved in performing or supervising the project (noting "contractor" as the position title if applicable). Furthermore, the CRA explicitly warns claimants that when signing the tax credit application, the taxpayer remains legally responsible for filing a compliant claim even if misled by third-party promotions.
The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Bar

One of the most unforgiving procedural provisions in Canadian tax law governs the SR&ED reporting deadline. The statutory expenditure reporting deadline sits in Subsection 37(11) of the ITA, while the investment tax credit reporting deadline sits in Paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in Subsection 127(9) (alongside Paragraph 149(1)(j) for exempt R&D corporations). Under these provisions, a claimant must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information within 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year.

Because Paragraph 150(1)(a) of the ITA sets a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date at 6 months after the end of its taxation year, the corporate SR&ED reporting window runs for an additional 12 months beyond the T2 due date, yielding an absolute statutory deadline of 18 months from the end of the taxation year in which the qualified expenditures were incurred. Crucially, there is no statutory mechanism in the ITA to extend or waive this 18-month deadline. Filing late results in the total and permanent loss of the SR&ED tax credit and pool deduction for the year, with no administrative relief available.
CRA Review Mechanics, Pre-Claim Advisory Services, and Dispute Resolution

Once a corporate SR&ED claim is filed, the CRA aims to process refundable claims within 60 to 180 calendar days, specifically targeting 60 calendar days for claims accepted as filed without audit and 180 calendar days for refundable claims selected for review. Published processing times exclude delays beyond the CRA's control, such as incomplete claims, claims filed without the corresponding income tax return, failure to respond to CRA information requests or proposal letters, postponed meetings, or prior-year SR&ED reviews affecting the current claim. When a claim is selected for detailed review, a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) evaluates the scientific and technological eligibility of the claimed work using the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, while a financial reviewer audits the claimed expenditures and tax schedules.

To assist businesses in assessing eligibility and documentation requirements prior to filing, the CRA offers several voluntary advisory and outreach mechanisms. The legacy Pre-Claim Project Review (PCPR) has been replaced by the Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC) and Pre-Claim Approval (PCA) services, which enable claimants to obtain free feedback or upfront eligibility approval from the CRA before submitting their tax return. However, as highlighted in the CRA's updated The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants, even claims that have been granted pre-claim approval may still be selected for post-filing review to verify the actual work performed and expenditures incurred. Additionally, the CRA operates the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS), the SR&ED Service Visit, and the SR&ED Outreach Program (including webinars and regional coordinating tax services office consultations) to educate innovative Canadian firms on record-keeping and eligibility standards. If a claimant disagrees with the CRA's findings during a review, it may escalate concerns under the Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns (issued August 18, 2020), and if a formal reassessment is issued, the claimant has the statutory right to file a Notice of Objection and subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal Stacking Mechanics

Provincial and territorial governments across Canada supplement the federal SR&ED program with jurisdiction-specific R&D tax credits and grants. While Prince Edward Island offers a 10% corporate investment tax credit on eligible property rather than a dedicated SR&ED credit, all other provinces and Yukon provide targeted R&D tax incentives. Apart from Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration), provincial R&D credits are harmonized with the federal SR&ED definition and are claimed directly on Schedule 5 of the federal T2 return.
Quebec: Transition from Legacy R&D Credits to the Unified CRIC Regime

Quebec administers an independent R&D tax incentive system through Revenu Québec. For taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025, Quebec's primary incentive was the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) claimed on Form RD-1029.7. Under Form RD-1029.7, corporations carrying on R&D in Quebec earned a refundable tax credit ranging from 14% to 30% (with the 30% enhanced rate available to CCPCs on up to $3 million of eligible R&D salaries and 50% of subcontractor costs, phasing down between $50 million and $75 million in prior-year worldwide assets), after deducting an asset-based exclusion threshold of at least $50,000 (scaling up to $225,000 for corporations with assets of $75 million or more).

For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 (including 2026 calendar-year filings), Quebec replaced Form RD-1029.7 and several ancillary R&D credits with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR. The CRIC provides a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures exceeding the corporation's exclusion threshold, and a 20% fully refundable tax credit on eligible expenditures above that $1,000,000 threshold, available to all corporations regardless of size or CCPC status, while also restoring eligibility for R&D capital expenditures.
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC Framework
Ontario offers three complementary R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), co-administered by the Ontario Ministry of Finance and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA):

The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), governed by Section 96 (specifically Subsections 96(3.1), 96(8), 96(12), and 96(14)) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and claimed on Schedule 566 (entered on Line 468 of Schedule 5), is an 8% refundable tax credit for qualifying corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario that carry on SR&ED in Ontario and file federal Form T661 and Schedule 31. Qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures, restored capital expenditures, and eligible repayments, up to an annual expenditure cap of $3,000,000 shared among associated corporations (yielding a maximum refundable credit of $240,000). The $3 million expenditure limit phases out when prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or when prior-year taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. (Although the 2018 Ontario Budget proposed a tiered 8% to 12% OITC rate based on R&D intensity effective March 28, 2018, that proposal was never enacted following the 2018 provincial election, and the statutory rate under Section 96 remains 8%, having previously been reduced from 10% in 2016). Under Subsection 96(14) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), a corporation may waive the current year OITC in whole or in part.

The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508, provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (reduced by any OITC and OBRITC claimed) that can be carried back 3 years or carried forward 20 years to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable. Additionally, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under eligible research contracts with Ontario Eligible Research Institutes up to a $20 million annual cap.
British Columbia, Alberta, and Other Provincial Jurisdictions
British Columbia (Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (B.C.), Form T666)

Governed by Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) and recently amended by Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026, the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit is administered by the CRA on behalf of the BC Ministry of Finance and claimed on Form T666 (attached to the top of the T2 return and entered on Line 659 for the non-refundable credit and Line 674 for the refundable credit of Schedule 5). Following the enactment of Bill 2 (2026), British Columbia harmonized its program fully with the federal Bill C-15 reforms.

Specifically, qualifying corporations that are CCPCs or Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with a permanent establishment in BC may claim a 10% refundable tax credit on the lesser of their SR&ED qualified BC expenditure for the tax year or their federal expenditure limit as defined in Subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) of the federal ITA. Effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, this refundable expenditure limit doubled from $3 million to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual BC refundable credit from $300,000 to $600,000), and the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range increased to $15 million to $75 million. All other qualifying corporations—as well as CCPCs and ECPCs on BC qualified expenditures exceeding their refundable limit, and active corporate members of partnerships claiming their proportionate share—may claim a 10% non-refundable tax credit (less any refundable credit claimed or amount renounced) to offset BC corporate tax payable. Bill 2 (2026) also removed the former September 1, 2027 sunset date and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024. Form T666 must be filed no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the qualified expenditures are incurred.
Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — Form AT1 Schedule 29)

Effective for taxation years beginning on or after January 1, 2021, Alberta offers the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) for SR&ED expenditures incurred in Alberta at a corporation's permanent establishment in the province. The IEG provides an 8% base refundable grant on qualifying Alberta SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's two-year average base spending level, plus a 12% incremental enhancement—yielding a combined 20% refundable grant—on qualifying expenditures exceeding the two-year average base up to an annual expenditure cap of $4,000,000 shared among associated corporations (for a maximum annual refundable grant of $800,000). Corporations with prior-year federal taxable capital between $10 million and $50 million see the IEG reduced on a sliding scale, and corporations with taxable capital at or above $50 million are completely ineligible for the IEG.

body.text: Assistance Grinding and Multi-Jurisdictional Stacking Mathematics

Under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Paragraph (h) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in Subsection 127(9), alongside Subsections 127(18) and 127(19) of the federal ITA, all provincial R&D tax credits and grants (as well as direct government grants, forgivable loans, and emergency wage subsidies) constitute government assistance. When the amount of assistance and contract payments relating to a project exceeds the SR&ED expenditures of the project, Subsection 127(19) reduces the qualified SR&ED expenditures of the claimant and any non-arm's-length party to nil. Consequently, a claimant must always calculate its provincial R&D tax credit first, and deduct that expected provincial credit from its federal Subsection 37(1) expenditure pool and its Subsection 127(9) qualified expenditures—including under the proxy method—before applying the 35% or 15% federal ITC rate.

body.text: Direct Federal Innovation Funding and Complementary Tax Incentives

Canadian R&D performers frequently combine SR&ED tax credits with direct federal grants, repayable contributions, procurement contracts, and clean economy investment tax credits. While stacking is legally permitted across these programs, any direct government assistance or contract payment received in respect of an SR&ED project reduces the federal Subsection 37(1) pool and Subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsections 127(18) and 127(19).
National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) and Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC)

The National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) and the Regional Development Agencies (RDAs) provide non-repayable R&D contributions for small and medium-sized Canadian enterprises with project funding thresholds of up to $10,000,000 per project. Because NRC IRAP directly reimburses a percentage of internal technical salaries and contractor costs, the IRAP grant constitutes government assistance under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(18), reducing the net qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for the 35% federal ITC while leaving the gross SR&ED salary base intact for computing the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount.

Complementing NRC IRAP, Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC)—administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)—functions as the federal government's procurement-innovation program for Canadian SMEs. Under the ISC Challenge Stream, participating federal departments fund Phase 1 proof-of-concept R&D up to $150,000 and subsequent Phase 2 prototype development awards. Depending on the legal structure of the ISC award, non-repayable grant awards reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures as government assistance, while R&D procurement contracts executed on behalf of the Crown reduce qualified expenditures as contract payments under Subsection 127(9).
Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) and Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits
Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) / Strategic Response Fund (ISED)

Launched in 2017 as part of the federal Innovation and Skills Plan and managed by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) (with certain pillars transitioning under the Strategic Response Fund banner), the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) was created to address structural weaknesses in Canada's industrial competitiveness, including an over-reliance on indirect tax incentives, low collaboration between large firms, SMEs, and academia, commercialization capital shortages, and the foreign acquisition of Canadian companies and intellectual property. Unlike NRC IRAP (which funds projects up to $10 million), SIF targets large-scale transformative investments requesting a minimum government contribution of $10,000,000, funding up to 50% of eligible project costs—including direct labour, overhead, subcontracts, direct materials and equipment, land and buildings, and other direct costs—through repayable and non-repayable contributions. Compliant with Canada's international trade agreements, SIF contributions are never contingent in law or in fact on export performance.
The SIF program architecture is organized into two macro-components spanning five distinct streams:

cells: Industrial R&D to test commercial potential of early concepts, adapt research findings into disruptive commercial products, or develop cleaner production processes.
Expansion or material improvement of existing industrial/technological facilities to increase manufacturing capacity, scale proven technologies, and improve production efficiency.
Securing new large-scale production or R&D mandates in Canada by multinational or domestic firms where the facility or mandate did not previously exist in Canada.
Industrial research and large-scale pre-commercial technology demonstration uniting private firms, SMEs, universities, and research institutes (competitive intake).
Supporting large-scale, high-impact pan-Canadian innovation networks that sub-allocate funding and strengthen national supply chains and commercialization linkages.

body.text: Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits (CT ITC and CTM ITC)

Co-administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and Natural Resources Canada (NRCan), the federal government has implemented major refundable tax credits supporting the clean economy transition, notably the Clean Technology (CT) Investment Tax Credit and the Clean Technology Manufacturing (CTM) Investment Tax Credit, each providing a refundable tax credit of up to 30% of project capital cost for eligible clean technology property and clean technology manufacturing machinery and equipment. Because a single depreciable asset cannot concurrently claim both a Clean Economy ITC and a restored SR&ED capital expenditure ITC, corporate tax planners must model whether an asset acquired after December 15, 2024, yields a higher net cash recovery under the 30% fully refundable CT/CTM ITC or under the SR&ED capital regime (where the 35% enhanced rate is 40% cash-refundable, yielding a 14% immediate cash refund plus a 21% non-refundable ITC and 100% Subsection 37(1) pool deduction).
Strategic Audit Defence and Compliance Conclusions

A comprehensive audit evaluation of Canada's post-2024 R&D tax architecture demonstrates an environment of expanded fiscal generosity paired with rigorous judicial and administrative enforcement. To maximize financial recovery while insulating claims against reassessment by CRA Research and Technology Advisors and Financial Reviewers, corporate claimants and tax practitioners must execute five interconnected compliance strategies.

First, corporate tax departments must enforce strict statutory rate and deadline precision across all filings. All financial models and Form T661 Part 5 calculations must apply the statutory 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) rate under ITR Subsection 2900(4) rather than outdated 65% or 60% figures. Concurrently, controllers must treat the 18-month corporate filing deadline under Subsection 37(11) and Paragraph 127(9)(m) as an absolute statutory bar with zero ministerial discretion for late-filing relief, establishing internal governance controls to submit complete Form T661, Schedule 31, and provincial credit schedules concurrently with the 6-month T2 return.

Second, scaling technology companies must actively optimize the post-December 15, 2024 expenditure limits and revenue elections enacted in Bill C-15. High-growth CCPCs that have raised substantial equity rounds exceeding $15 million in prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada should evaluate filing the Subsection 127(10.31) or (10.32) election to compute their $6 million expenditure limit under the ECPC three-year average annual revenue method in Subsection 127(10.6), thereby preserving up to $2.1 million in 100% refundable federal cash credits. Simultaneously, Canadian public corporations meeting ECPC criteria (in both federal and harmonized British Columbia filings) must transition from non-refundable 15% claims to claiming the 35% federal and 10% BC refundable credits on up to $6 million of qualified expenditures, while associated CCPC and consolidated ECPC groups must execute mandatory allocation agreements under Subsections 127(10.3) and 127(10.62) prior to filing.

Third, claimants must calibrate their annual overhead election around cloud computing intensity and restored capital assets. Because cloud computing and software subscriptions are not separately claimable under the proxy method, data analytics, artificial intelligence, and compute-intensive enterprises whose incremental cloud and facility overhead exceeds 55% of their direct SR&ED salary base should deliberately elect the Traditional Method and maintain itemised allocation keys. Concurrently, hardware, manufacturing, and life sciences firms must segregate depreciable R&D equipment acquired and leased after December 15, 2024, to capture restored capital ITCs under the 90% ASA test (Line 390, removing those assets from Schedule 8 CCA) or the 25%/25% Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) rules (Line 504).

Fourth, technical authors preparing Part 2, Section B of Form T661 must anchor Line 242, Line 244, and Line 246 narratives in objective state-of-the-art benchmarks. In light of recent Tax Court of Canada dismissals (Dave's Diesel, JEC Distributors, Logic Data Products, and Paveit Construction), Line 242 must never frame technological uncertainty around the subjective skill limitations of internal personnel or the mere commercial absence of a product on the market. Instead, within the 350-word limit per section, the narrative must objectively establish why publicly accessible engineering standards, published scientific literature, and commercially available tools known to competent professionals in the field were fundamentally incapable of resolving the underlying system or component conflict without systematic hypothesis formulation and experimental testing.

Finally, R&D performers must institutionalize contemporaneous experimental record-keeping alongside rigorous payroll compliance. Engineering teams should continuously archive dated hypothesis-testing evidence, experimental test matrices, failed trial telemetry, and project time records as work progresses to satisfy the "How" requirement of the 2021 CRA Guidelines. Simultaneously, finance teams must verify prior to tax year-end that all accrued SR&ED wages are paid within the 180-day window under Subsection 78(4), that specified employee remuneration excludes bonuses and adheres to the 2.5 × YMPE and 75% proxy salary base caps under ITR Subsection 2900(7), and that provincial credits—including Quebec's new CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR), Ontario's OITC/ORDTC, BC's expanded T666 credit, and Alberta's IEG—are accurately deducted as government assistance prior to computing the final federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit.
